title: 14-Year-Old Girl Riding Home on a School Bus Killed by Saudi Coalition Strike in Yemen

_Story by Rachid Mohsen*_

SANA'A, Yemen--On the afternoon of October 5, 14-year-old Athir al-Amri had
just taken the last exam of her first semester. She was on a school bus going
home when an airstrike hit next to the bus as it drove through the Saawan area
of eastern Sana'a, Yemen's capital. Shrapnel struck her in the head, killing
her, witnesses and relatives said.

"She was planning to spend the holiday playing as all children do during
school breaks," her 35-year-old cousin, Mohammed Al-Lahida, told Drop Site
News. "The shrapnel decapitated her. If her mother saw her body, she would die
of grief."

Two of her classmates were also wounded, one of them gravely, in the strike by
the Saudi-led coalition.

Ansarallah, an armed group also known as the Houthis, seized the capital
Sana'a in 2014. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015 on the side of
Yemen's internationally recognized government. A civil war raged for eight
years, killing tens of thousands and sparking one of the world's worst
humanitarian crises, until a fragile ceasefire was brokered in 2022.

The civil war reignited in July when Saudi Arabia carried out airstrikes to
prevent an inbound Iranian passenger plane from landing in Ansarallah-
controlled Sana'a. In response, Ansarallah declared a maritime blockade on all
Saudi-linked vessels in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, one of the world's busiest
shipping lanes.

The fighting escalated sharply last month when Ansarallah swept down the Red
Sea coast, overcoming Saudi-backed government forces and capturing the key
port city of Mokha as well as islands in the Bab el-Mandab Strait, allowing
them to tighten their declared blockade of Saudi shipping. Saudi Arabia and
its allied forces in Yemen then embarked on a military offensive to retake the
territory, launching airstrikes on Ansarallah along the Red Sea coast and
other areas controlled by the group, including Sana'a. Ansarallah responded by
escalating missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia.

The Saudi-led coalition's Colonel Turki Al-Maliki [said on October
5](https://x.com/CJFCSpox/status/2107034669305004345) that 100 fighter jets
took part in [Operation Dawn of Yemen](https://www.dropsitenews.com/p/saudi-
yemen-ansarallah-us-strike-caribbean-boat-bolsonaro-brazil-election) and
destroyed 324 "high-value targets," including weapons depots, boat explosives
storage and naval mines. He described them as "legitimate military targets
belonging to the terrorist Houthi militia."

Brigadier General Yahya Saree [said on X
](https://x.com/Yah_Saree/status/2107876034137985392)on October 7 that the
Saudi coalition had carried out 1,798 airstrikes and missile attacks since the
escalation began, concentrated on Sanaa, Taiz, Marib, and Al-Jawf. On October
6 and 7, Ansarallah [fired ballistic
missiles](https://x.com/Yah_Saree/status/2108027458796863609) at Abha
International Airport in Saudi Arabia's Asir region and at King Khalid
International Airport in Riyadh, killing three people, wounding dozens, and
disrupting operations, the coalition said,
[accusing](https://x.com/CJFCSpox/status/2107937711009181749/photo/1) the
Houthis of "terrorist attacks on civilians and civilian objects in the
kingdom."

Almost 1,000 people have been killed in the latest fighting, most of them
fighters, with over 200,000 displaced, according to the United Nations. Al-
Amri is among 83 civilians killed and 146 wounded in Ansarallah-controlled
areas since the escalation began in September, Dr. Anees Al-Asbahi,
spokesperson for the Ansarallah health ministry, told Drop Site News, around
60% of them women and children.

## **" Shrapnel tore through the vehicle"**

Rehab Al-Jaafari and Reem Al-Wakedi, both also 14 years old, were on the bus
with al-Amri. Al-Jaafari's father, Bassem, told Drop Site News they were the
only three girls left on the bus when the strike happened. Al-Jaafari told her
father they had asked the driver to stop and wait when the first missile hit
near the Atiya petrol station nearby.

"He told them not to worry and sped on to reach safety. As the bus passed a
Houthi compound that was being targeted, a second missile struck and shrapnel
tore through the vehicle. Rehab pulled the classmate beside her down beneath
the seat. Athir was sitting in the back row," the father said.

Al-Jaafari woke up later in the back of a Houthi military pickup truck, one of
several military vehicles that carried the wounded to Al-Nubala Hospital. Al-
Wakedi sustained moderate injuries to her arm and was in the emergency room
having her wounds dressed. Before she went into intensive care, Al-Jaafari
asked her father where the other girls were. Bassem told his daughter that al-
Amri was being treated on another floor. He did not tell her she had been
killed.

Al-Jaafari had shrapnel lodged in her back and lost the sight in her right
eye. A wound to her face damaged her ear and left her unable to open her mouth
properly. She remains on intravenous fluids and is vomiting whatever she eats.
Doctors removed shrapnel from her right arm, and a wound to her right foot
means it will be some time before she can walk. The hospital discharged her on
October 6, according to her father, though she requires continued medical
care.

## **No Shelter**

On October 3, a strike near al-Sabeen Hospital for Maternity and Childhood in
Sana'a [damaged](https://x.com/TvAlmasirah/status/2106413096961024386) the
facility's windows, medical equipment, and medicine supplies, and injured 10
staff and patients, the health ministry's Al-Asbahi told Drop Site.

A nurse, Aisha Mohammed, said her right arm was broken when a door fell on
her. Window glass shattered and breathing equipment flew across the room.
"Premature babies and infants in incubators were among the most exposed,"
Mohammed said. The next day, on October 6, warplanes flew over again, causing
some patients to flee the hospital.

Only about 60% of Yemen's health facilities are fully functioning, and
comprehensive trauma and emergency care is available at about 6% of those
assessed, [according](https://www.emro.who.int/media/news/who-scales-up-
health-response-in-yemen-as-escalating-conflict-strains-already-fragile-
health-system.html) to the World Health Organization (WHO).

"Our hospitals cannot withstand this kind of attack," Al-Asbahi said, warning
that hospitals rely on generators that need scarce fuel.

Residents say the launch of ballistic missiles from inside the city brings its
own terror. At dawn on October 8, people woke to a huge blast that many
thought was a strike. It was a missile launched from near Sana'a airport,
residents said.

Wesam Ahmed, who works for a company delivering goods from Jeddah--Saudi
Arabia's second-largest city--to Sana'a, said strikes damaged its office in
Attan, southwest of Sana'a. He said he has suspended work and lost hundreds of
customers.

Tawfiq al-Hamidi, head of the Geneva-based SAM Organization for Rights and
Liberties, which documents violations in Yemen, said the Saudi-led strikes
have hit populated areas in broad daylight. The internationally recognized
government has
[warned](https://x.com/Yem_army_media/status/2107133287768490180) residents to
stay away from Ansarallah military sites.

"But in Sana'a, avoiding every site linked to the group could mean avoiding
large parts of the city, which has no civil defense system or shelters to
speak of," al-Hamidi said.

_* The reporter has been granted anonymity because of the security situation
in Yemen. Rachid Mohsen is a pseudonym._
